content.text: {"primary_meaning":"In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the fear of the LORD' is understood not primarily as terror but as reverent awe, worshipful respect, and humble submission before God — an attitude of devotion and obedience that Scripture presents as the foundation ('beginning') of wisdom and knowledge and the proper posture of covenant relationship with God.","primary_basis":["Proverbs 1:7 ('The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge')","Proverbs 9:10 ('The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom')","Psalm 111:10","Job 28:28","Ecclesiastes 12:13 ('Fear God and keep his commandments')","Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:12","Proverbs 8:13 ('The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil')","Proverbs 14:26-27","Psalm 34:11","Isaiah 11:2-3 (the Spirit of 'the fear of the LORD' resting on the Messiah)","Acts 9:31","2 Corinthians 7:1"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Filial fear versus servile fear: a classical Catholic and scholastic distinction (Augustine, Aquinas) in which mature 'fear of the LORD' is filial reverence born of love (a gift of the Holy Spirit, cf. Isaiah 11:2), while servile fear — dread of punishment — is an imperfect, preparatory stage.","basis":["Isaiah 11:2-3","1 John 4:18 ('perfect love casts out fear')","Psalm 130:4","Catechism of the Catholic Church on the gifts of the Spirit"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Covenant loyalty and obedience: especially in Deuteronomic usage, 'fearing the LORD' functions as near-synonymous with keeping the covenant — loving, serving, and obeying God — rather than an emotional state.","basis":["Deuteronomy 6:13; 10:12-13","Deuteronomy 5:29","Joshua 24:14","Ecclesiastes 12:13"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Literal dread or terror before God's holiness and judgment: some interpreters (and many biblical-theology treatments) insist the term retains a real element of trembling and fright before the numinous holiness of God, resisting the softening of 'fear' into mere respect.","basis":["Exodus 20:18-20","Isaiah 6:5","Hebrews 10:31 ('a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God')","Hebrews 12:28-29","Luke 12:4-5","Philippians 2:12"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Ethical avoidance of evil: fear of the LORD read chiefly as a moral disposition — hating and turning away from sin — emphasized in wisdom literature.","basis":["Proverbs 8:13","Proverbs 16:6","Job 1:1; 28:28"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"'God-fearers' as a sociological/technical category: in Second Temple and New Testament contexts, 'those who fear God' can denote Gentile adherents to the synagogue, a usage distinct from the symbolic-theological meaning.","basis":["Acts 10:2, 22","Acts 13:16, 26"],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"This term has one of the more settled interpretive consensuses in biblical studies: reverent awe leading to wisdom and obedience. The main live debate is not over the core meaning but over emphasis — how much genuine 'trembling' the term retains versus how fully it should be rendered as 'reverence' or 'awe.' The alternatives listed are largely complementary emphases rather than mutually exclusive readings, and most traditions (Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox) hold them together. The filial/servile distinction is standard in Catholic moral theology; the covenant-obedience reading dominates Old Testament scholarship on Deuteronomy; the 'real dread' emphasis appears in some Reformed and biblical-theology writing."}
